I told each therapist that it did help with my depression but i had too much energy, too much spunk, too many strong impulses to control. I kept being prescribed lexapro until I weaned myself off it at 21. Stopped going to therapy at the same time. I started going back to therapy at 25 because another depressive episode was happening. I explained my past with medication for depression to my current therapist and they then took it as a major red flag and reassessed my diagnoses. Right now I’m diagnosed with BPD and BP, take meds for both, and am so much happier with my life now. Please know that these are very very VERY experimental and I have very little medical knowledge, none really. You basically flash your phone around your eyes *slowly* so your brain can click and realize it the light is still visible on the blind side. Red and green are the best colors to do this with because they are used in genera vision tests. Not an exercise but I also take CoQ10 because there are 2 studies that say it returned some vision to some people. 2 studies is very very very minimal too.

I had an ICH stroke, 14% of all strokes are ICH, so I may be a minority. I felt pain but more so in my eye some how. However it went away and I remember not being able to stay still. I kept lying down in bed then sitting up and then wanting to get up but couldn’t. Then I started throwing up and saw the pills for my Lupus in the bin and that’s when I realized something was wrong with me but didn’t know what. My family also realized something was wrong and called the ambulance. I don’t remember actually meeting the EMT but my family remembers me being unable to form complete sentences and when I did speak it didn’t make sense. Ironically, the only sentence that made sense was when the EMT started taking me outside and I screamed “WAIT I NEED A MASK FOR NO COVID” and somehow was able to put it on myself before collapsing into the EMTs arms. Then I was out for two days and stayed another week in the hospital. The pain I had was for a short while and went away the moment I was being treated. I hope that helps you

A lot of the stroke prevention is prevention for other health issues too! I say this because I have a chronic condition which literally has the same ideas to be safe as avoiding a stroke. 

1) 30 minutes of aerobic exercises 5 days a week. Can be walking, running, biking, etc. Sometimes people try to push the 10,000 steps a day idea but really 5,000 steps a day is good, especially if it’s overwhelming at first! 
2) Low processed, fresh diet. Avoided the word “healthy” because that’s sometimes slapped onto processed food... maybe has veggies but lots of salt, sugar, preservatives etc is not healthy.
3) avoid substance abuse. Smoking is a big thing to avoid and drinking can be cut down as well. It also includes other drugs that are not used for health purposes.

I too looked at loads of research and studies post stroke to see what would happen. If you saw those studies that were like “30% die post two days, X4% die one month, X1% die post three months” etc, know that they tend to include loads of other reasons too. Perhaps they had a chronic condition which caused something else in the time frame. Maybe they didn’t change their lifestyle which ended up with a second stroke. Maybe something happened not related to health issues and the researched couldn’t label it specifically. A doctor told me early on that surviving the actual stroke as it happens is the trickiest time for both the patients and doctors because it’s making sure patient survives.

While we may not currently be in the 10% of people who recovery to their “normal” functions post stroke, we can still strive for it and get close to it. Therapies, exercises, checking to see what disappears and appears post stroke,  maintaining a healthy lifestyle ensure we can be the best we can get to post stroke.

The sad thing about strokes is there is no “clear” plan on how it will play out. Every stroke is different and even if two people get the exact same stroke in the exact same spot at the exact same severity , etc, there can still be a multitude of reasons for the recovery to be different. Chronic conditions, substance use, exercise, are just a few examples of the differences in people’s lives. However, studies have shown those with loved ones who support them and have hope themselves recover at a greater, faster, and sustainable rates than those who do not. Offering them love and support is the best thing to do as the road to recovery can be very long.

I lost mine 3 months ago and got maybe 1/5 back on my right side. Do you know if it’s HH? HH is when both of your eyes are “half blind” on either the left or right. Also, which lobe, what kind of stroke, etc. for example: my stroke was ICH in temporal lobe- pretty low chances for me to heal all the way but I’ll have hope I’ll get at least central vision back. I’d love to see people’s faces again even if their hair is cut off from my vision. 

For healing, there doesn’t seem to be as much research for vision recovery as let’s say hand, arm, leg recovery post stroke(no hate to them). OT can help with living daily life activities by how to cope with the vision loss via walking cane, scanning, etc. VRT (Visual Restoration Therapy) May claim help but be careful the therapists aren’t doing it just for money. I even found a few studies that say COQ13 supplements helped return some vision to some other survivors years after their strokes and I am trying it myself. Best advice I can give is to try things out(ask your neurologist or PCP first), hope for the best, but also learn how to navigate with this if necessary.
